Internal Agency Delegations, A further tool that may enable 
administrations to avoid Senate involvement in the appointments process 
is the use of statutory authority to delegate the functions of a vacant office 
to a designated official. See, e.g., 6 U.S.C. § 112(b)(1), which provides that 
the Secretary of Homeland Security “except as otherwise provided by [the 
Homeland Security] Act, may delegate any of the Secretary’s functions to 
any officer, employee, or organizational unit of the Department.” In the 
words of Anne Joseph O’Connell, the contemporary scholar who has 
studied most extensively the use of acting government officials, 
[Djelegation of authority often acts as a complete (or nearly complete) 
substitute for acting officials.” Anne Joseph O’Connell, Actings, 120 
COLUM. L. Re v . 613, 682 (2020). It is thus not uncommon to see on an 
agency’s organization chart an official carrying a title that includes some 
version of “performing the duties of,” e.g., at the Department of Education 
in 2024, “Tisamarie Sherry, M.D., Ph.D., Performing the Delegable Duties 
of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation.”
Two scholars have even shown how the use of delegated authority may 
effectively create independent agencies inside larger units:
[Tn|he buck does not always stop with secretaries and 
commissioners. Rather, these leaders often relinquish their 
decisionmaking authority to their subordinates. In other words, 
they subdelegate their power—^not only to fellow political 
appointees, but often to tenure-protected career staff. These 
sub delegations are sometimes legally enforceable, but even when 
they are not, norms and resource constraints often result in 
effectively final, discretionary authority below agency heads.
Brian D. Feinstein & Jennifer Nou, Submerged Independent Agencies, 171 
U. Pa . L. Re v . 945, 949 (2023). Among the examples Professors Fein stein 
and Nou highlight to demonstrate the potential scope of such delegations 
is the decision of the Administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety 
Administration’s to assign rulemaking authority to a career Associate 
Administrator. As they explain:
The action gave the civil servant the authority “to exercise the 
powers and perform the duties of the Administrator” to “set[ ] 
motor vehicle safety and theft prevention standards” as well as 
“fuel economy standards.” Notably, the NHTSA Administrator 
reserved the authority to issue, amend, or revoke final rules 
concerning safety and fuel economy standards, but did not do so 
for theft prevention standards.
Id,
The FVRA on its face appears to accommodate the use of delegated 
authority to continue the functions of a PAS office that has become vacant.
